info_tile.heading: What is MVPF?
info_tile.description: The Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) is a metric that measures the social welfare benefit of a policy per dollar of government spending. It is a ratio that represents how much value beneficiaries receive relative to what the policy costs. See: [Policy Impacts Library, MIT](https://policyimpacts.org/mvpf-explained/what-is-the-mvpf/).
info_tile.formula:
Most MVPF work looks at policies where the person subject to the policy is also the main beneficiary, such as cash transfers. Detention is different. Jail is imposed on detainees but is justified as benefiting the general public. That is why this tool tracks both Detainee effects and broader Society effects when calculating the MVPF of detention.  
 Understanding MVPF requires not just technical knowledge, but also careful consideration of the ethical and empirical challenges inherent in valuing complex social outcomes. We hope this tool facilitates more informed and nuanced discussions about pre-trial detention policy.
info_tile.application_label: Our Approach to Cook County Jail
info_tile.application: In most MVPF work, people plug in causal estimates for how behavior changes at the intensive margin (for example, working a bit more or less when a benefit changes). For Cook County Jail, we do not have credible intensive-margin estimates for detention, and the policy questions we are interested in are about the extensive margin and the scale of the jail itself: who is detained at all, for how long, and what level of funding or even continued operation is justified. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework. This MVPF calculator for Cook County Jail is built to help you see how assumptions about extensive-margin harms and benefits feed into both the numerator and the denominator, using 2018 jail spending as the benchmark.  For a fuller discussion of this choice and its limits, see the [MVPF Explained](#mvpf-explained) tab.

scenario_selector.label: Select Scenario to calculate the MVPF:

scenarios.description:
The scenarios below offer three different set-ups for how to value the effects of detention on detainees. They differ only in how detainee harm is measured between two options, and whether spillover harms to the detainee’s community are included as well. 
 
Note: There are nearly infinite reasonable normative stances one could take about how to scale the harm of detention to detainees, especially in the absence of a clean experiment. The scenarios in this dashboard do not claim to identify a single “correct” stance. We do suggest a baseline scenario as a useful starting point, but it is only one choice among many reasonable alternatives. Instead, the dashboard provides a structured way to translate different views about detainee harm into concrete MVPF calculations so that policy and value disagreements can be discussed using the same underlying quantities.
scenarios.label: Select Scenario:

baseline.description: This baseline scenario values detainee harm using the Relative Harm Valuation (RHV) scale and does not include a separate community spillover term. It is the default specification in the dashboard and the recommended starting point for interpretation.

most_conservative.description: This scenario values detainee harm using Willingness to Pay for Freedom (WTP), which produces a smaller per-day harm estimate than RHV, and it does not include a separate community spillover term.

least_conservative.title: Upper-Bound Anchor / Largest Valuation
least_conservative.description: This scenario values detainee harm using RHV and adds a separate component for spillover harms to the detainee’s community.

analysis_parameters.heading: Analysis Parameters
analysis_parameters.description: You can adjust several parameters that act as multipliers to the components in the MVPF set-up. These inputs scale the numerator and denominator components of the MVPF and let you test how sensitive the results are to policy or system changes. The defaults for each parameter capture the picture of Cook County Jail in 2018. The other options available are outer bounds for sensitivity analysis, and some alternatives based on our broad review of the literature.

limitations.heading: Limitations and Considerations
limitations.intro: This dashboard is a structured way to translate assumptions into an MVPF for pretrial detention. It is not a definitive estimate of detention's "true" social value.
items: Normative choices drive results: the largest source of variation is how detainee harm is monetized (RHV vs WTP) and whether additional community spillovers are added.
Crime impacts are uncertain and context-dependent; in this dashboard, crime effects can affect both the numerator (social harms/benefits) and the denominator (public costs or savings).
Local transferability is limited: baseline costs and operating conditions are anchored to Cook County Jail in 2018 and may not generalize to other years or jurisdictions.
Component coverage is incomplete: the MVPF includes only impacts with usable estimates, so some downstream, distributional, or hard-to-monetize effects may be missing.

Marginal vs. average effects: we use annual totals rather than clean intensive-margin estimates, so the MVPF should be interpreted as a comprehensive assessment of extensive-margin policy rather than a traditional marginal policy change.
Parameter interactions: changing multiple parameters at once can produce compounding effects that are not always intuitive or linear.

what_is_mvpf.heading: What is MVPF?
what_is_mvpf.description: The Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) is a metric that measures the social welfare benefit of a policy per dollar of government spending. It represents how much value beneficiaries receive relative to what the policy costs. (Hendren and Sprung-Keyser 2020) See: [Policy Impacts Library, MIT](https://policyimpacts.org/mvpf-explained/what-is-the-mvpf/).

applying_to_detention.heading: Applying MVPF to detention in Cook County Jail
applying_to_detention.paragraph1:
Most MVPF work looks at policies where the person subject to the policy is also the main beneficiary, such as cash transfers. Detention is different. Jail is imposed on detainees but is justified as benefiting the general public. That is why this tool tracks both Detainee effects and broader Society effects when calculating the MVPF of detention. (Dobbie and Yang 2021; Stevenson and Mayson 2022)

In most MVPF work, people plug in causal estimates for how behavior changes at the intensive margin (for example, working a bit more or less when a benefit changes). For Cook County Jail (abbreviation: CCJ), we do not have credible intensive-margin estimates for detention, and the policy questions we are interested in are about the extensive margin and the scale of the jail itself: who is detained at all, for how long, and what level of funding or even continued operation is justified. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework. This CCJ calculator is built to help you see how assumptions about extensive-margin harms and benefits feed into both the numerator and the denominator, using 2018 jail spending as the benchmark. (Hendren and Sprung-Keyser 2020; Dobbie, Goldin, and Yang 2018)
applying_to_detention.paragraph2: In most MVPF work, people plug in causal estimates for how behavior changes at the intensive margin (for example, working a bit more or less when a benefit changes). For Cook County Jail, we do not have credible intensive-margin estimates for detention, and the policy questions we are interested in are about the extensive margin and the scale of the jail itself: who is detained at all, for how long, and what level of funding or even continued operation is justified. It uses the full annual costs of operating the jail and the full set of impacts on people who are detained to summarize those tradeoffs in an MVPF-style framework. This CCJ calculator is built to help you see how assumptions about extensive-margin harms and benefits feed into both the numerator and the denominator, using 2018 jail spending as the benchmark.
applying_to_detention.paragraph3: To further understand the assumptions behind this approach, we provide a detailed breakdown of each scenario, the parameters, and how they may reflect the broader implications of detention policy. The scenarios and parameters are designed to explore different perspectives on the tradeoffs between public costs and the various social, individual, and government-related harms and benefits associated with detention. Each scenario allows users to adjust key components, such as the detainee value approach, and the parameters allow users to change the multipliers applied to these components, helping to assess the sensitivity of the MVPF to these assumptions. By reviewing the full explanations below, users can better understand the rationale behind the assumptions and how small changes in these variables can lead to different policy recommendations. This will give you a comprehensive view of the complexities and trade-offs inherent in making decisions about the scale and impact of pretrial detention. (Stevenson and Mayson 2022)

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.description: This dashboard helps policymakers and researchers understand the tradeoffs involved in pretrial detention by quantifying both costs and benefits in a common framework. We use Cook County Jail in 2018 as our base case.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.description: The MVPF calculation combines the net value of detention on detainees and society and then divides by the public cost of detention to provide a comprehensive view of detention's impact:
methodology.component1: Detainee Values: Quantifying the harm imposed on individuals through detention
methodology.component2: Society Values: Measuring external impacts on public safety and community wellbeing
methodology.component3: Government Costs: Calculating the full fiscal burden of detention operations

data_sources.title: Data Sources
data_sources.description: This analysis relies on empirical evidence from Cook County Jail operations (2018), academic research on detention impacts, and validated cost estimates from government budgets and policy studies.

sections.label: Description
sections.text: The proportion of detainees charged with at least one felony.

sections.label: Default
sections.text: 70% felonies (30% misdemeanors).

sections.label: Use in MVPF
sections.text: Scales crime effects in the numerator and crime-related costs in the denominator, because felony and misdemeanor offenses differ in both social harm and government cost. A higher felony share generally shifts the MVPF further from 1 when a non-zero crime effect is selected (the direction depends on the sign of the crime effect).

sections.label: Explanation and Alternatives
sections.text: We set the default to 70% felonies based on Illinois evidence that pretrial detention is felony-dominant (about 82% felony among the pretrial jail stock in 2019). Because stock measures overstate felony share relative to annual admissions (which include more short-stay misdemeanors), we lower the default to 70%. The dashboard allows 50% to 100% felonies to explore sensitivity.

sections.label: Notes and Key Assumptions
sections.text: We assume one charge per detainee, using the highest-level charge when multiple charges exist. This may undercount social harm more than associated government costs because the marginal difference of the harm of an additional crime is likely larger than that of the cost of processing an additional charge. This biases the MVPF away from 0 when crime effects are non-zero (baseline sets crime effects to 0). When crime effects are applied, felony vs. misdemeanor values are built from granular crime-type estimates (McCollister 2008) using equal-incidence averaging across crime types, which is inexact but preserves magnitude and broad severity differences.

sections.label: Description
sections.text: The number of people detained pretrial for at least one night over the course of the year.

sections.label: Default
sections.text: 33,945 admissions (100%).

sections.label: Use in MVPF
sections.text: Scales the total value in the numerator (detainee harms and societal effects). Operational funding is treated as fixed and does not scale with this parameter.

sections.label: Explanation and Alternatives
sections.text: We source this from the Cook County Jail dashboard, which distinguishes bookings (about 100,000 in 2018) from admissions (33,945), where admissions reflect bookings that result in at least one night in custody. The dashboard allows a multiplier range of 80% to 120% to explore how detention scale affects the MVPF.

sections.label: Notes and Key Assumptions
sections.text: In reality, some operating costs likely vary with detainee volume. Because we do not have a credible marginal cost estimate for Cook County Jail, we treat 2018 operating costs as fixed. This is a meaningful limitation and will bias the MVPF away from 1 whenever population is set above or below the default.

sections.label: Description
sections.text: The assumed impact of detention on detainees’ future crime (two-year rearrest), expressed as a percentage-point change.

sections.label: Default
sections.text: 0% change.

sections.label: Use in MVPF
sections.text: Determines the sign and scales the crime-related components in the numerator (societal value of crime effects) and in the denominator (government costs or savings associated with crime effects).

sections.label: Explanation and Alternatives
sections.text: We set the baseline to 0 because the best causal evidence does not support a clear non-zero net effect of pretrial detention on crime. The leading study (Dobbie, Goldin, and Yang, 2018) reports a point estimate and a 95% confidence interval wide enough to allow both modest crime reduction and modest crime increase. The dashboard offers the point estimate (5%) and the CI bounds (−4%, +14%) as sensitivity options.

sections.label: Notes and Key Assumptions
sections.text: This parameter is framed as the crime-type mix of the current detainees (e.g. CCJ 2018), and makes an assumption that that mix is directly related to the crime-type mix of the hypothetical increase or decrease of crime as a result of the detention. This is a big assumption that may not be supported by the literature, so we recommend adjusting this parameter as needed to change the multiplicative effect on the crime components. Additionally, note that the crime components themselves assume symmetry: the value of a crime prevented equals the harm of a crime that occurs (same magnitude, opposite sign), and government savings from a prevented crime equal government costs of an additional crime. Detention could decrease crime via incapacitation or deterrence, or increase crime by disrupting employment, housing, and social ties after release.

sections.label: Description
sections.text: The average number of days detainees are held.

sections.label: Default
sections.text: 70 days.

sections.label: Use in MVPF
sections.text: Scales time-based detainee harms and (if included) community spillovers. Operational funding is treated as fixed and does not scale with length of stay.

sections.label: Explanation and Alternatives
sections.text: The CCJ dashboard reports a 60.37-day average for releases in 2018, which likely understates overall detention exposure because it excludes long-stay detainees not released during the year. We correct for this by setting a 70-day baseline informed by a long-stayer dataset. The dashboard offers the 60-day release-based figure, our 70-day baseline, and up to 203 days (the long-stayer average) to examine sensitivity.

sections.label: Notes and Key Assumptions
sections.text: For details on the long-stayer dataset and the construction of the 70-day baseline, see the Overleaf documentation and OSF page. [link] [link]

baseline.title: Baseline Scenario
baseline.description: In this scenario, detainee harm is valued using the Relative Harm Valuation (RHV) scale. RHV yields a relatively large negative value per day in custody based on an indirect survey of the general population. We do not add any spillover harms to the detainee’s community, on the view that some of those broader harms may already be reflected in RHV. This combination leans on components that are well supported in the literature and keeps extra assumptions to a minimum. It is the default scenario in the dashboard and our recommended starting point for interpretation.

most_conservative.title: Lower-Bound Anchor / Smallest Valuation
most_conservative.description: In this scenario, detainee harm is valued using the smaller Willingness to Pay for Freedom (WTP) scale rather than the larger Relative Harm Valuation (RHV) scale. WTP is based on direct survey responses from people who have experienced jail, producing a much smaller per-day harm estimate than RHV (roughly 300x smaller). Because this scale assigns far less harm to detention, the numerator becomes less negative and the MVPF moves closer to zero. This anchor represents the most detention-favorable valuation of harm in the dashboard.

least_conservative.title: Upper-Bound Anchor / Largest Valuation
least_conservative.description: In this scenario, detainee harm is valued using the same RHV scale as in the baseline anchor, and we add an extra term to capture spillover harms to the detainee’s community that are not already captured by the individual-level value. This additional component makes the total harm assigned to detention larger in magnitude. As a result, the numerator becomes more negative and the MVPF for detention moves further below zero. Among the scenarios, this anchor represents the least detention-favorable valuation of harm.

detainee_values.title: Detainee Values
detainee_values.description: Detainee Values capture the total harm detention imposes on people who are jailed. We measure this using a willingness-to-pay lens, estimating how much a person would trade to avoid being detained. This reflects short-term harms, disruptions to work and family life, and long-term effects on health, income, and stability.

harm_valuation.button_text: Willingness to Pay derived from Relative Harm Valuation
harm_valuation.explanation: The baseline detainee component, which measures harm by comparing each day in custody to crime-victimization cost benchmarks such as robbery or aggravated assault. This produces a larger per-day harm value than detainee self-reported WTP (~$4,000/day), and scales with whatever length of stay (non-linearly), population, or charge mix the user chooses. Because it reflects broader social harm rather than ability-to-pay limits, it is used as the default. Source: crime-harm equivalence estimates from Stevenson & Mayson (2022).

wtp_freedom.explanation: An alternative detainee valuation based on stated willingness-to-pay (WTP) per day to avoid jail, drawn from surveys of people facing detention. Valued at $11/day in 2018 dollars. This approach reflects detainees' own monetary tradeoffs and can be scaled using any assumed length of stay or detainee population. It typically produces much smaller harm estimates than the baseline Relative Harm Valuation, which makes the overall MVPF less negative and is therefore a more conservative choice. Source: detainee WTP evidence summarized in Stevenson & Mayson (2022).

society_values.title: Society Values
society_values.description: Society Values measure how detention affects external factors like public safety, victimization risk, and community wellbeing. These values summarize the effects felt by people outside the jail and convert those effects into a common dollar scale for comparison.

crime_prevention.explanation: An optional component that assigns a social value to crimes prevented (or a social cost to crimes increased) due to detention. We value this using McCollister (2008) per-crime social cost estimates, which convert changes in crime counts into dollars reflecting victim harms and broader social costs. This component is off in the baseline (set to zero) because the most credible causal evidence on pretrial detention does not support a clear, generalizable crime-reduction effect. It is only activated when you turn on the Crime Effect assumption parameter. Once activated, the MVPF can move in either direction: assuming detention prevents crime makes the MVPF less negative, while assuming it increases crime makes it more negative. The size of that shift also depends on the crime mix parameter, since the McCollister (2008) dollar values differ by offense type, so we apply different values for misdemeanors versus felonies.

court_appearance.explanation: Included as a baseline society component because court appearance is a central justification for pretrial detention. This component places a dollar value on avoiding failures to appear (FTA) by combining administrative costs of warrant issuance and possible rearrest with an assumed FTA probability. Source: Fishbane, Ouss & Shah (2020) and Cook County court data.

community_spillovers.explanation: An optional component that captures spillover harms of detention on families and communities, such as disrupted caregiving, household production, and informal economic support. This component is not included in the baseline and is set to zero unless turned on. When included, it is a negative per-detainee value, making the MVPF more negative. Our current approach uses a Wrongful Death Damages (WDD) economic-loss anchor to monetize the scale of household disruption: we take the economic-loss portion of wrongful death settlements and rescale it to a typical detention spell, applying a conservative 25% external-share to avoid double counting the detainee’s own losses. Spillover effects reflect the impacts detention itself and do not scale with any downstream crime assumptions.

government_cost.title: Government Cost
government_cost.description: Government Cost reflects all public spending required to run the detention system. This includes daily operations, staffing, healthcare, facilities, court processing, and administrative overhead. It represents the fiscal cost taxpayers bear to support the current level of detention.

operational.explanation:
The baseline government cost component, representing the full operating budgets for the Cook County Department of Corrections and Cermak Health Services. These expenses include staffing, food, medical care, housing, and other daily operations, and they can be allocated over any assumed detainee count or length of stay. Since these costs reflect actual fiscal outlays, they form the default denominator of the MVPF. Source: Cook County FY2018 Appropriation Budget. 

Note: We exclude other potential government cost channels, such as downstream public health use or conviction-related administrative costs, due to limited credible estimates. This omission likely understates total government costs and biases the MVPF modestly toward zero.

crime_decrease.explanation:
An optional component that captures changes in government spending associated with changes in crime induced by detention. This component is off in the baseline and is only activated when the Crime Effect assumption parameter is turned on. We value these costs or savings using McCollister (2008) government cost estimates, which translate changes in crime into public-sector expenditures such as policing, courts, and corrections. Values are scaled by crime type, so shifts toward felonies versus misdemeanors have larger fiscal effects. 

This component moves in lockstep with the crime effect in the numerator: if detention is assumed to reduce crime, government costs fall and the MVPF becomes less negative; if detention is assumed to increase crime, government costs rise and the MVPF becomes more negative.

sensitivity_analysis.title: Sensitivity Analysis
sensitivity_analysis.description: This section lets you see how the MVPF for pretrial detention changes when you vary one parameter at a time, holding all else equal. The visualizations show how different assumptions about felony rate, detainee population, crime effects, and length of stay shift the overall result. Use this tab to see which conclusions are robust across parameter changes and which depend heavily on specific assumptions.

felony_rate.title: Felony Rate Sensitivity
felony_rate.description: This chart shows how the MVPF changes when varying the felony rate assumption while holding all other parameters constant. The felony rate represents the percentage of detainees who would have committed a felony if not detained. Higher felony rates suggest greater crime prevention value from detention, which can increase the MVPF by reducing societal costs of crime.

detainee_population.title: Detainee Population Sensitivity
detainee_population.description: This chart shows how the MVPF changes when varying the detainee population multiplier while holding all other parameters constant. The population multiplier scales the baseline number of detainees, allowing you to assess how different jail population sizes affect the cost-effectiveness of pretrial detention. Changes in population directly affect both the total costs and total impacts.

crime_effect.title: Crime Effect Sensitivity
crime_effect.description: This chart shows how the MVPF changes when varying the crime effect assumption while holding all other parameters constant. The crime effect represents the percentage change in crime rates attributable to detention. Negative values indicate crime increases (due to destabilization), zero indicates no effect, and positive values indicate crime decreases (due to incapacitation). This parameter affects both social benefits and government costs.

length_of_stay.title: Length of Stay Sensitivity
length_of_stay.description: This chart shows how the MVPF changes when varying the average length of stay while holding all other parameters constant. Length of stay measures how many days, on average, individuals spend in pretrial detention. Longer stays increase both the harms to detainees and the operating costs to government, while potentially providing more time for crime prevention effects.

overview_intro.title: Calculating the MVPF for Cook County Jail
overview_intro.paragraph1:
This calculator lets you explore how different assumptions change the Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) for pretrial detention in Cook County Jail. 

 You can adjust several inputs that determine the number of people detained, the composition of cases, and the average length of stay. These inputs reshape the numerator and denominator of the MVPF and let you test how sensitive the results are to policy or system changes. Use these scenarios and parameters to see how alternative value judgments and crime assumptions shift the MVPF and what that implies about the social return of pretrial detention under different assumptions.
overview_intro.paragraph2:
Select your preferred MVPF scenario. In every scenario, the numerator is built from two types of components: 
 • harms to detainees, valued in dollars per day in custody, 
 • effects on society, such as changes in court appearance or crime outcomes as a result of detention.
overview_intro.paragraph3: The denominator is always the 2018 operating cost of the jail, scaled by the population and length of stay choices you set above, plus any costs or savings associated with crime outcomes.
overview_intro.paragraph4: The scenarios below offer three different approaches to detainee harm. You may choose the baseline approach, switch to the smaller detainee harm value, or include additional spillover harms to the detainee's community.

mvpf_purpose.title: How to use this result
mvpf_purpose.content:
This is the Marginal Value of Public Funds (MVPF) for pretrial detention under the assumptions you selected above, expressed as a ratio of total dollar-valued harms and benefits to the public cost of operating the jail. 
 • To understand what is driving the result, review the numerator and denominator breakdown below; 
 • to test sensitivity, change one parameter at a time or switch scenarios and compare how the breakdown changes, 
 • or go to the “Compare alternative scenarios” tab for a summary of how your calculated MVPF would change if you vary one aspect at a time while holding all others fixed..

scenarios_intro.title: Sensitivity analysis
scenarios_intro.content: Overview of the Scenario Analysis tab, explaining what users can explore and learn from the visualizations below.

alt_scenarios.title: Alternative Scenarios Description
alt_scenarios.paragraph_1: This tab lets you compare how the MVPF for pretrial detention changes across alternative valuation scenarios and parameters. The scenario determines what components will be included to quantify the MVPF, and the parameters are the multipliers on those components.
alt_scenarios.paragraph_2: This tab is dynamic, meaning the outputs change based on the choices made on the Calculation tab. The chart to the left shows you how *your MVPF* would have changed had you picked the same parameters but a different scenario. The graphs below show you how *your MVPF* changes if you modify one parameter, but hold all else equal.
alt_scenarios.paragraph_3: Use this tab to see which conclusions are robust across scenarios and which depend heavily on specific normative and policy choices.

parameter_intro.title: Parameter Selection
parameter_intro.paragraph_1: Use these controls to adjust several parameters that act as multipliers to the components in the MVPF set-up. The defaults for each parameter capture the picture of Cook County Jail in 2018. The other options available are outer bounds for sensitivity analysis, and some alternatives based on our broad review of the literature. Changing parameters updates the underlying inputs, while scenarios change which components are included and how they are valued.

scenario_intro_p1: The three scenarios differ only in how we value harm to detainees (a larger Relative Harm Valuation scale versus a smaller survey-based "Willingness to Pay for Freedom") and whether we add an extra negative term for spillover harms to the detainee's community. In all scenarios, the crime effect components are set to zero by default; they only change if you adjust that parameter elsewhere in the dashboard.

data_sources.title: Data Sources
data_sources.content: This analysis relies on empirical evidence from Cook County Jail operations (2018), academic research on detention impacts, and validated cost estimates from government budgets and policy studies. Key data sources include the Cook County Jail dashboard for admissions and population statistics, the Cook County FY2018 Appropriation Budget for operational costs, and peer-reviewed research on detention effects including Dobbie, Goldin, and Yang (2018) for crime effects, Stevenson & Mayson (2022) for harm valuation approaches, McCollister et al. (2008) for crime cost estimates, and Fishbane, Ouss & Shah (2020) for court appearance data.

about_ccj.title: About Cook County Jail
about_ccj.content: Cook County Jail is one of the largest single-site pretrial detention facilities in the United States, located in Chicago, Illinois. In 2018, the jail had approximately 33,945 admissions (individuals detained for at least one night), with an average length of stay around 70 days. The facility serves as the primary pretrial detention center for Cook County's criminal justice system, housing individuals awaiting trial who have not been released on bail or their own recognizance. The jail is operated by the Cook County Sheriff's Office, with healthcare services provided by Cermak Health Services.

contact.title: Contact
contact.content: For questions about this tool, methodology, or data sources, please contact the development team at the University of California, Berkeley. For questions about Cook County Jail operations or data, please contact the Cook County government directly.

acknowledgements.development: This data tool was developed by Adrienn Sinapis J. and Lara Pesce Ares, as part of the 'Building Data Products for Public Impact' clinic led by Diag Davenport at the University of California, Berkeley. It is intended to support evidence-based policymaking and research on criminal justice reform. We gratefully acknowledge the contributions of researchers, data scientists, and policy experts who made this work possible.
acknowledgements.framework: This tool builds upon the MVPF framework applies it to the context of pretrial detention. We acknowledge the foundational research in criminal justice, welfare economics, and public policy that informs our methodology.
acknowledgements.data_access: We thank Cook County government agencies for providing access to administrative data and operational information. This project also benefited from open-source software tools and libraries that enable interactive data visualization and analysis.

disclaimer.title: Disclaimer
disclaimer.content: The views and findings presented in this tool are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the official positions or policies of Cook County government, funding organizations, or affiliated institutions. All estimates should be interpreted as analytical tools to inform discussion rather than definitive policy prescriptions.
